A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAPS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison, including matching material relocated between pages.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention-head mappings, correlation and causal-ablation experiments, multi-token generalization tests, and human evaluation of generated head descriptions.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical studies, revises experimental results, expands multi-token evaluation, and adds validation of previously unrecognized name-copying heads.

M1.justification: The vocabulary projection, predefined-relation score, normalized saliency measure, and GPT-4o interpretation pipeline remain unchanged. Newly discussed hallucination-mitigation techniques are future-work suggestions, not implemented components.

E1.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 24 expand multi-token evaluation from three relations to eleven. Added coverage includes copying, name copying, letter extraction, year succession, and additional semantic relations, substantially broadening the tasks tested under multi-token inputs. The main single-token datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The comparison methods remain self-only attention, random-head ablation, randomly initialized head matrices, and the global/specific-head references. Comparisons with heads identified by Wang et al. and Merullo et al. are retained; changes to control-task selection concern evaluation design.

E3.justification: The principal correlation experiment changes from one prompt template to four, with scores computed separately for each template. Appendix D adds a restricted-attention validation and contrasting-prompt case study. Causal control-task counts also change, including Pythia 12B copying from zero to three controls; the causal prompts in Table 18 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Multi-token robustness testing expands substantially. Appendix D newly examines whether additional MAPS name-copying heads reflect genuine capabilities or inaccurate classifications, using dynamic correlations and a prompt-dependent example for GPT-2 small head 8.11. Table 25 also supplies two additional qualitative head examples.

E5.justification: Table 24 replaces individual correlation p-values with a single reported upper bound of 9.3e-4, reducing statistical detail. Five repetitions and standard-deviation reporting for random-head ablations remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Correlation values throughout Tables 1 and 8–17 are revised alongside the expanded prompt protocol. Causal results also change: Pythia 12B copying base/target-ablated/random-ablated accuracies change from 0.65/0.34/0.79 to 1.00/0.68/1.00, without an explained protocol revision. Table 24 expands from nine to 32 model–relation rows, and Appendix D adds a 0.94 correlation for additional name-copying heads.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations, relation and saliency definitions, and Appendix F metrics are retained. The existing dynamic relation-score formula receives an equation number in v2; no new derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: parameter-based functionality inference, correlation and causal relevance, broader head discovery, and automated descriptions supported by human judgment. The added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds an explanation linking name-copying behavior to context-dependent attention, distinguishing capability from activation on a particular prompt. The limitations expand the explanation of early-layer coverage, and Appendix E discusses possible ways to reduce hallucinated descriptions.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 supplies the four correlation templates, Appendix D specifies prompts and attention restrictions for its new validation, and Appendix C explains the GPT-2 xl last-letter exclusion. Existing MAPS hyperparameters, software, hardware, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Five references are added to support the proposed hallucination-mitigation directions, including Kuhn et al., Azaria and Mitchell, and Gur-Arieh et al. The principal related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain stable.

P1.justification: There are localized wording and typo corrections, revised experimental descriptions, and added explanatory paragraphs in the limitations and appendices. The section sequence and most existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: Table 24 is expanded and restructured, removing its individual p-value columns. Table 25 grows from three to five head examples, while the prompt table and other appendix displays move. Existing figures are retained, with limited layout changes and repagination.

improvement.justification: The broader multi-token tests and direct validation of additional name-copying heads strengthen support for generalization and help address possible false positives. These are useful, bounded gains. Reporting remains imperfect: four-template aggregation and substantial causal-score revisions are insufficiently explained, and Table 24 loses individual p-values.
